# File path built from HTTP request data (Node.js)

`qualor:js/path-traversal` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-22](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A01:2025 Broken Access Control](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/), [A01:2021 Broken Access Control](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
HTTP request data that reaches a file-system path (Express, Fastify, Next.js):

- the path of the `fs` and `fs/promises` functions that read, write, create, list, delete, move or
  change files (`readFile`, `writeFile`, `createReadStream`, `unlink`, `rm`, `readdir`, ...), and
  the second path of `copyFile`, `rename` and `link`;
- Express's `res.sendFile()` and `res.download()` without the `root` option.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
`path.join(base, name)` does not keep the result inside `base`: a name such as `../../etc/passwd`
climbs out of it, and `path.resolve()` with an absolute name drops the base altogether. A client
can then read secrets and source code, overwrite files the application trusts, or delete data.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the requested name is joined to a directory and sent.

```javascript
const express = require('express');
const path = require('path');

const app = express();

app.get('/reports', (req, res) => {
  res.sendFile(path.join(__dirname, 'reports', req.query.name));
});
```

**Compliant:** with the `root` option, Express keeps the resolved path inside that directory.

```javascript
const express = require('express');
const path = require('path');

const app = express();

app.get('/reports', (req, res) => {
  res.sendFile(req.query.name, { root: path.join(__dirname, 'reports') });
});
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Serve files with the `root` option of `res.sendFile()` or `res.download()`.
- For other file operations, keep only the last segment with `path.basename()` (and reject `.` and
  `..`), or map the request value to a file name through an allow-list.
- If a path must be built, resolve it and check that it still lies inside the base directory
  before using it.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Express
- Next.js
- Fastify
- Node.js fs

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- A check after resolving the path (`if (!full.startsWith(base)) return`) is not recognised, nor
  is a ternary that returns the request value after an `includes()` check; `path.basename()`,
  number conversions and allow-list lookups are.
- A record looked up in a server-side store with a request value as its key
  (`sessions.get(req.cookies.session).id`) counts as request data.
- `stat`, `lstat`, `access`, `exists` and `realpath` are not checked: they only tell whether a file
  exists, and `realpath()` is how a path is checked.
- `fs` functions are recognised through `require()` and `import` of `fs` and `fs/promises`;
  `fs-extra` and other file libraries are not checked.
- `res.sendFile()`/`res.download()` are checked on a second handler parameter named `res`,
  `resp`, `response`, `_res` or `_response`; a `root` that itself comes from the request is not
  checked.
- An allow-list lookup is recognised only in a `const` table with literal keys and values in the
  same file.
- Request handlers are recognised by the name of their second parameter: a handler written as
  `(request, out)` is not checked.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test files [`rules/js/path/path-traversal.js`](../../../rules/js/path/path-traversal.js) and [`rules/js/path/path-traversal.ts`](../../../rules/js/path/path-traversal.ts) hold every case the rule reports or accepts:
